questions.question: How is the rank of a matrix read from its reduced row echelon form?
options: Count the entries in the last row only.
questions.explanation: In reduced row echelon form, each nonzero row contains a pivot and zero rows contain none. Therefore the number of nonzero rows equals the rank.
questions.source_support: Definition of rank.
questions.review_notes: Manually designed in LA high-quality batch 7; concept-specific stem and plausible distractors.
questions.skill_detail: conceptual: Definition of rank.
option_explanations: A zero column has no pivot, but counting zero columns measures neither the number of pivots nor the rank.
One pivot entry per nonzero row is counted; additional entries equal to $1$ can occur and would overcount.
The last row alone cannot reveal pivots in earlier rows, so it cannot determine the rank.

questions.question: What does rank measure informally?
options: How many row operations have been performed, in every case without exception.
How many entries the matrix has in total.
How large the largest entry is.
How many independent pieces of information the matrix contains.
questions.explanation: Rank counts independent row or column directions, equivalently the dimension of the range. Informally, it measures how many independent pieces of information survive.
questions.source_support: Interpretation of rank.

option_explanations: Different row-reduction paths may use different numbers of operations while leaving the rank unchanged.
An $m\times n$ matrix always has $mn$ entries, but those entries may encode highly dependent rows or columns.
Scaling a matrix can make entries arbitrarily large without changing any dependence relation or the rank.

questions.question: What is the rank of a zero matrix?
questions.explanation: A zero matrix reduces to itself and has no pivot and no nonzero row. Hence its rank is $0$.
questions.source_support: Example: a zero matrix has rank $0$.

The number of columns is the rank only for full column rank, whereas a zero matrix has no independent column.
The number of rows is the rank only for full row rank, whereas every row here is the zero vector.

questions.question: What is the rank of the identity matrix $I_n$?
questions.explanation: The identity $I_n$ is already in RREF and has one pivot in each of its $n$ rows and columns. Therefore its rank is $n$.
questions.source_support: Example: $I_n$ has rank $n$.

Rank $0$ would mean no pivots, but $I_n$ has all $n$ diagonal pivots.
Rank $1$ is correct only for $I_1$; for general $I_n$ there are $n$ pivot rows.

questions.question: For an $m\times n$ matrix, which upper bound on rank is always valid?
options: $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ must be larger than both $m$ and $n$.
questions.explanation: There can be at most one pivot per row and at most one pivot per column. Thus $\operatorname{rank}(A)\le m$ and $\operatorname{rank}(A)\le n$.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: rank is bounded by rows and columns.
questions.review_notes: Manually designed in LA high-quality batch 7; concept-specific stem and plausible distractors.

questions.skill_detail: conceptual: Key result: rank is bounded by rows and columns.
option_explanations: The product $mn$ counts entries; for example a nonzero $2\times2$ rank-one matrix has rank $1$, not $4$.
A rank larger than both dimensions would require more pivots than there are rows and columns.
Since rank is at most $\min(m,n)$, it certainly cannot exceed the larger quantity $m+n$.

questions.question: What is the rank of $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&3\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$?
questions.explanation: The displayed matrix is in echelon form with pivots in its first two rows and a zero third row. It therefore has exactly two nonzero pivot rows and rank $2$.
questions.source_support: Definition of rank from RREF.
questions.review_notes: Manually designed in LA high-quality batch 7; concept-specific stem and plausible distractors.
questions.skill_detail: application: Definition of rank from RREF.
option_explanations: Rank $1$ counts only one pivot, but the leading $1$s in columns $1$ and $2$ are two distinct pivots.
Rank $3$ incorrectly counts the zero third row; that row contributes no pivot.
Rank $0$ would require every row to be zero, contrary to the first two pivot rows.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: A square $n\times n$ matrix has full rank exactly when it is:
questions.explanation: A square matrix is invertible exactly when it has a pivot in every row and column, which is exactly full rank $n$.
questions.skill_detail: full rank iff invertible
questions.source_support: A square matrix has full rank iff it is invertible (nonzero determinant).
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Singular means non-invertible and rank below $n$, so it is the opposite of the full-rank condition.
Symmetry does not guarantee rank: the symmetric zero matrix is singular.
Triangular form alone is insufficient; a triangular matrix with a zero diagonal entry can be rank deficient.

questions.question: An $m\times n$ matrix has full column rank when its columns are:
questions.explanation: Full column rank means every column is a pivot column, equivalently the columns admit no nontrivial linear relation and are linearly independent.
questions.skill_detail: full column rank meaning
questions.source_support: Full column rank means linearly independent columns.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: All-zero columns span only $\{0\}$ and give rank $0$, not full column rank.
Two identical nonzero columns satisfy $c_1-c_2=0$, so they are linearly dependent.
Unit length alone does not ensure independence: two identical unit columns both have length $1$ but are dependent.

questions.question: If an $m\times n$ matrix has full row rank, then $Ax=b$ is solvable:
questions.explanation: Full row rank means rank $m$, so the column space is all of $\mathbb R^m$. Therefore every compatible right-hand side $b$ lies in the range and $Ax=b$ is solvable.
questions.skill_detail: full row rank meaning
questions.source_support: Full row rank makes $Ax=b$ solvable for every compatible $b$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: The homogeneous system $Ax=0$ is solvable for every matrix, but full row rank also makes every nonzero $b\in\mathbb R^m$ reachable.
Full row rank makes the range the entire codomain, so claiming that no $b$ is reachable reverses the conclusion.
A rectangular $m\times n$ matrix with $m\le n$ can have rank $m$ and solve every right-hand side; squareness is unnecessary.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has rank $2$. Is it invertible?
options: No, because it does not have full rank
Yes, because its rank is positive
questions.explanation: A $3\times3$ matrix is invertible only at rank $3$. Rank $2<3$ leaves a nontrivial kernel, so the matrix is not invertible.
questions.skill_detail: rank vs invertibility instance
questions.source_support: A square matrix is invertible iff it has full rank.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Positive rank only says the map is not zero; rank $2$ still falls short of the required rank $3$.
Being square is necessary for a two-sided inverse but not sufficient; rank must also equal the size.
A rank-deficient square matrix has determinant $0$, not $2$, and determinant $2$ would actually imply invertibility.

questions.question: How is rank related to the range of the corresponding linear map?
options: It is always one less than the dimension of the range.
It equals the dimension of the range.
It is unrelated to any linear map.
It equals the dimension of the kernel in every case.
questions.explanation: The columns of the matrix generate the image of the associated linear map. The number of independent image directions is therefore both the matrix rank and the dimension of the range.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: rank equals the dimension of the range.

questions.question: Why should rank not be read by simply counting nonzero rows in the original matrix?

Original nonzero rows are never changed by row operations.
Row reduction may reveal that some original nonzero rows are dependent.
Only zero rows can contain pivots.

questions.explanation: Rank is the number of nonzero rows in the unique RREF. Identical RREFs therefore have identical pivot counts and the same rank.

questions.explanation: The second row is twice the first, so it adds no independent direction. Row reduction gives one nonzero row, hence rank $1$.

questions.question: For an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ plus the dimension of the kernel equals:
questions.explanation: Rank-nullity for the map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ gives $\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim\ker A=n$, the dimension of the domain and number of columns.

Rank and nullity are nonnegative and sum to $n$, so the sum is zero only in the zero-dimensional domain case.
